problem: The sign is wrong. Substituting the diameter d = 2a into A = πa² gives A = πd² = 4πa², which is four times the true area, so R_r comes out sixteen times too large, not too small. As written, a student who makes this slip is told the opposite of what actually happens.
fix: A diameter used where the radius belongs makes the area four times too large, and after squaring makes R_r sixteen times too large. Using the wire radius makes it far too small.

problem: "Raises radiation resistance by μ_eff² and raises the received voltage in the same way" reads as if the voltage also rises by μ_eff². R_r goes as A², so it rises by μ_eff²; the open-circuit received voltage goes as the effective area, so it rises only by μ_eff. The two factors are different.
fix: Since R_r goes as A², the rod raises the radiation resistance by μ_eff², while the open-circuit received voltage rises by only μ_eff, in proportion to the effective area A_eff = μ_eff A.

problem: "Even a λ/10 loop would be tens of metres across" overstates the size. At 1.6 MHz, λ/10 is 19 m of circumference, about 6 m across; only at the bottom of the band does the diameter reach roughly 18 m.
fix: Even a λ/10 loop would be several metres to nearly twenty metres across — impossible inside a radio set.

problem: A = C²/(4π) holds only for a circle, so the C-only formula is for a single-turn circular loop. The text says just "for a single turn", which invites its use for square or rectangular loops.
fix: For a single-turn circular loop, putting A = C²/(4π) turns this into a formula in the circumference alone.
